I can’t access the web or current pediatric guideline documents right now, so I cannot provide up‑to‑date guideline citations or a definite diagnosis. I also cannot safely diagnose your child remotely. Below is concise, general urgent‑care guidance you can use tonight.

Immediate red flags — go to the nearest emergency department or call emergency services now if any of these are present:
- Trouble breathing, noisy breathing, wheeze, or swallowing difficulty; or swelling of the face, lips, or tongue.
- Very sleepy, hard to wake, confused, floppy, or not interacting normally.
- Severe or worsening neck stiffness, severe headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, or fainting.
- Rapidly spreading rash with many small purple or red spots that do not fade/“blanch” when you press a glass against them (possible petechiae/purpura).
- High fever (very hot to touch) that is not responding to antipyretic measures and the child looks very unwell.
- Hives plus any breathing or circulatory symptoms (possible anaphylaxis).
- Signs of poor perfusion: pale/ mottled/ cool extremities, very fast or very slow heart rate, or very low urine output.

If none of the red flags above are present tonight:
- Contact your child’s pediatrician or an urgent care for same‑day advice and likely in‑person evaluation tomorrow. If you cannot reach them, consider urgent care.
- Keep the child comfortable and hydrated. Offer fluids frequently. Monitor temperature and behavior.
- You may give age‑appropriate fever‑reducing medication only if you have been previously advised it’s safe for your child; follow the dosing instructions on the product label or your clinician’s prior instructions. Do not give aspirin to children.
- Avoid applying topical agents to the rash unless advised by a clinician.

What I cannot do here:
- I cannot provide a definite diagnosis (many causes — viral exanthems, bacterial infections including strep or scarlet fever, allergic reactions, and rarer but serious causes — can present with fever and rash).
- I cannot cite current guideline sources right now because I cannot access the web.

If you want more specific advice tonight, provide brief details (how the rash started and looks — flat vs raised, blistering, location, whether it blanches with pressure; current temperature; breathing; activity level; any known exposures or recent illnesses/vaccines/medications). I cannot diagnose, but additional details can help indicate whether urgent evaluation is needed.
